```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "H")

```
```{r data, include=FALSE}
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

setwd("C:/Users/Gebruiker/OneDrive - Erasmus University Rotterdam/Seminar DSMA/Decision Trees and Ensembles")
load("Churn.RData")
churn_rate <- mean(data$Churn == "Yes")  # this is the overall churn rate: 0.375 or 37.5%
```
```{r data split, include=FALSE}
set.seed(123)
train_rows <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$Churn),
                            function(rows) sample(rows, round(0.7 * length(rows))))) # 70% of churners and 70% of non-churners
train <- data[train_rows, ]
test  <- data[-train_rows, ]
```
```{r grow tree, include=FALSE}
full <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0, xval = 10))
rpart.plot(full)
```
```{r tune tree, include=FALSE}
cp_table <- full$cptable
row_min <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), ] # row with min. cross-validated error
row_1se <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= row_min["xerror"] + row_min["xstd"])[1] # row number of tree chosen by 1-SE rule
cp_1se <- cp_table[row_1se, "CP"]
```
```{r prune tree, include=FALSE}
tree <- prune(full, cp = cp_1se) # full tree pruned back to chosen cp
var_importance <- round(100 * tree$variable.importance / sum(tree$variable.importance), 1) # variable importance in %
```
```{r predictions test set, include=FALSE}
test_pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")

conf_matrix <- table(Predicted = test_pred, Actual = test$Churn)
acc_test <- mean(test_pred == test$Churn)
acc_baseline <- mean(test$Churn == "No")
acc_train <- mean(predict(tree, train, type = "class") == train$Churn)
acc_full <- mean(predict(full, test, type = "class") == test$Churn)
conf_matrix; acc_test; acc_baseline; acc_train; acc_full

sensitivity <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "Yes"]) # churners detected
specificity <- conf_matrix["No", "No"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "No"])   # stayers cleared
sensitivity; specificity

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x) # for easier writing in text section, shows percentages directly

```

# 1. Introduction

Customer churn (customers leaving for a competitor) is costly for telecom providers: acquiring a new customer costs more than retaining one, and customers become more profitable the longer they stay (Gupta et al., 2006). This report analyses the churn behaviour of `r format(nrow(data), big.mark = ",")` customers of a telecom provider. Because the provider wants insight into *why* customers leave, not just a black-box prediction, a **classification tree** is used, which predicts churn with transparent if-then rules that managers can act on (James et al., 2013; Yildirim & Kübler, 2023).

# 2. Data

For each customer, the data contain *Churn* (yes/no; `r format(sum(data$Churn == "Yes"), big.mark = ",")` customers or `r pct(churn_rate)` churned) and twelve predictors without missing values: contract term (*Contract*; 59.7% month-to-month), *tenure* (1--72 months), *MonthlyCharges* (\$18--\$119), *TotalCharges*, *Partner*, *PhoneService*, *MultipleLines*, *InternetService* (DSL, fibre optic or none) and four add-ons (*OnlineSecurity*, *OnlineBackup*, *DeviceProtection*, *TechSupport*; "No internet service" for the 19.4% without internet). A stratified split (seed 123; Section 3) gives a **training set of `r format(nrow(train), big.mark = ",")`** and a **test set of `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` customers**, both with a churn rate of `r pct(mean(test$Churn == "Yes"))`; always predicting "no churn" thus gives a baseline test accuracy of `r pct(acc_baseline)`.

# 3. Methods

Consider a data set of $n$ observations with a categorical response $Y$ with classes $k = 1, \dots, K$ and predictors $X_1, \dots, X_p$. The tree is fitted and evaluated in five steps (James et al., 2013; Tan et al., 2014).

1. **Train/test split.** The data are divided into a training set (70%) for fitting and tuning, and a test set (30%) used only to estimate out-of-sample performance. The split is *stratified*: 70% of each class is drawn at random, so both sets keep the class proportions.
2. **Growing the tree.** CART (Breiman et al., 1984), implemented in `rpart` (Therneau & Atkinson, 2023), grows the tree top-down by *recursive binary splitting*. For each node $m$, every predictor $X_j$ and cut-point $s$ (or grouping of categories) is tried, and the split into $\{X_j < s\}$ and $\{X_j \geq s\}$ that most reduces the weighted Gini impurity $G_m = 1 - \sum_k \hat p_{mk}^2$ of the two child nodes is chosen, where $\hat p_{mk}$ is the share of class $k$ in node $m$. Splitting continues until nodes are pure or too small; each leaf predicts its majority class, with $\hat p_{mk}$ as class probability.
3. **Cost-complexity pruning.** A fully grown tree fits noise in the training data (overfitting). It is therefore pruned by minimising $R_{cp}(T) = R(T) + cp \cdot |T| \cdot R(T_{\text{root}})$, where $R(T)$ is the training misclassification error of subtree $T$, $|T|$ its number of leaves and $R(T_{\text{root}})$ the error without splits. The **complexity parameter** $cp$ is the price of an extra leaf: a split is kept only if it lowers the relative error by at least $cp$. $cp = 0$ keeps the full tree; larger $cp$ gives smaller, nested subtrees.
4. **Tuning $cp$.** The training set is split into $K = 10$ folds. For every candidate $cp$, the tree is grown and pruned on nine folds and its error is measured on the tenth; averaging over folds gives the cross-validated error (*xerror*) and its standard error (*xstd*). The **one-standard-error (1-SE) rule** selects the simplest tree whose xerror is within one standard error of the minimum (Hastie et al., 2009), favouring a simpler, more interpretable tree.
5. **Prediction and evaluation.** Each test observation is passed down the pruned tree and assigned the majority class of its leaf (for two classes: predicted probability above 0.5). Performance is measured by accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, and compared with a majority-class baseline. Variable importance is a predictor's total impurity reduction, including as a surrogate split.

# 4. Results

**Tuning.** The full tree has `r max(cp_table[, "nsplit"])` splits and a cross-validated relative error of `r sprintf("%.3f", cp_table[nrow(cp_table), "xerror"])`. The error is lowest (`r sprintf("%.3f", row_min["xerror"])`) at `r row_min["nsplit"]` splits; larger trees fit noise (Appendix A, Table A1). The 1-SE rule selects $cp$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", cp_1se)`: a tree with **`r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"]` splits and `r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"] + 1` leaves** (xerror `r sprintf("%.3f", cp_table[row_1se, "xerror"])`, Figure 1).

**Interpretation.** *Contract* is the root split and the most important variable (`r var_importance["Contract"]`% of importance), followed by *tenure* (`r var_importance["tenure"]`%) and *TotalCharges* (`r var_importance["TotalCharges"]`%; Table A2). The main rules are:

1. **One- or two-year contracts:** 40% of customers, only 10% churn.
2. **Month-to-month, fibre optic, tenure under 16 months:** the highest-risk group (18% of customers, 81% churn).
3. **Month-to-month fibre, longer tenure:** churn depends on price; 62% for monthly charges of at least \$95.55, and 30--63% below that, depending on charges.
4. **Month-to-month DSL or no internet:** 28% churn after 6 months' tenure, but 63% for newer customers without online backup.

```{r tree plot, fig.width=8, fig.height=2.7, out.width="100%", fig.cap="Pruned tree. Each node shows the predicted class, the churn probability and the share of training customers."}
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)
```

**Test-set performance.** The pruned tree classifies **`r pct(acc_test)`** of the `r format(nrow(test), big.mark = ",")` test customers correctly, against the `r pct(acc_baseline)` baseline. Training accuracy is similar (`r pct(acc_train)`), and the unpruned tree reaches only `r pct(acc_full)`. It detects **`r pct(sensitivity)`** of churners (sensitivity; `r conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"]` of `r sum(conf_matrix[, "Yes"])`) and correctly clears **`r pct(specificity)`** of non-churners (specificity; `r conf_matrix["No", "No"]` of `r sum(conf_matrix[, "No"])`).

# 5. Conclusions and Discussion

A pruned nine-leaf tree predicts churn of unseen customers with `r pct(acc_test)` accuracy (baseline `r pct(acc_baseline)`). Churn is driven mainly by **commitment** (contract), **customer lifetime** (tenure) and **price and service** (fibre internet, monthly charges and add-ons). Three actions follow: (1) encourage month-to-month customers (55% churn) to move to longer contracts (10%); (2) prioritise new fibre-optic customers (81% churn) with onboarding support; and (3) review prices for long-standing fibre customers and promote add-ons such as online backup to new DSL customers.

**Limitations.** The tree misses `r pct(1 - sensitivity)` of churners (a lower cut-off catches more, with more false alarms); single trees are unstable, so cut-points are approximate; and the rules show associations, not causes.

# Appendix A

**Table A1.** Cost-complexity table of the full tree (selected rows, 10-fold cross-validation). Errors are relative to the root-node error; the 1-SE rule selects $cp$ = `r sprintf("%.4f", cp_1se)` (`r cp_table[row_1se, "nsplit"]` splits).

```{r cp table}
cp_rows <- cp_table[, "nsplit"] <= 25 | cp_table[, "nsplit"] == max(cp_table[, "nsplit"])
cp_summary <- data.frame(cp = sprintf("%.4f", cp_table[cp_rows, "CP"]),
                         Splits = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"],
                         Leaves = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"] + 1,
                         round(cp_table[cp_rows, c("rel error", "xerror", "xstd")], 3))
names(cp_summary)[4:6] <- c("Training error", "CV error", "CV std. error")
knitr::kable(cp_summary, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
```

**Table A2.** Relative variable importance in the pruned tree (percentage of total; includes surrogate splits).

```{r importance table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable = names(var_importance),
                        `Importance (%)` = var_importance, check.names = FALSE),
             format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Appendix B

The code below reproduces all numbers, tables and figures in this report (R 4.3.3, `rpart` 4.1.23).

\setlength{\parskip}{0pt}

\begin{lstlisting}[
basicstyle=\ttfamily\fontsize{6}{6.4}\selectfont,
columns=fullflexible,
breaklines=true,
breakatwhitespace=false,
keepspaces=true,

frame=none

# 1. Packages: rpart fits CART trees, rpart.plot draws them
library(rpart); library(rpart.plot)

# 2. Load the data (data frame `data`: 4,000 customers, 13 variables)
setwd("C:/Users/Gebruiker/OneDrive - Erasmus University Rotterdam/Seminar DSMA/Decision Trees and Ensembles")
load("Churn.RData")
churn_rate <- mean(data$Churn == "Yes")  # this is the overall churn rate: 0.375 or 37.5%

# 3. Stratified 70/30 split: 70% of the churners and 70% of the non-churners go to the
#    training set, so both sets keep the 37.5% churn rate; the seed makes it reproducible
set.seed(123)
train_rows <- unlist(lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(data)), data$Churn),
                            function(rows) sample(rows, round(0.7 * length(rows))))) # 70% of churners and 70% of non-churners
train <- data[train_rows, ]                          # 2,800 training customers
test  <- data[-train_rows, ]                         # remaining 1,200 test customers

# 4. Grow the full tree: cp = 0 switches off pruning, xval = 10 stores the
#    10-fold cross-validated error (xerror) for every cp value
full <- rpart(Churn ~ ., data = train, method = "class",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0, xval = 10))
rpart.plot(full)

# 5. Tune cp with the 1-SE rule: smallest tree whose CV error is within
#    one standard error (xstd) of the minimum CV error
cp_table <- full$cptable
row_min <- cp_table[which.min(cp_table[, "xerror"]), ] # row with min. cross-validated error
row_1se <- which(cp_table[, "xerror"] <= row_min["xerror"] + row_min["xstd"])[1] # row number of tree chosen by 1-SE rule
cp_1se <- cp_table[row_1se, "CP"]

# 6. Prune the full tree back to the chosen cp and compute variable importance
tree <- prune(full, cp = cp_1se) # full tree pruned back to chosen cp
var_importance <- round(100 * tree$variable.importance / sum(tree$variable.importance), 1) # variable importance in %

# 7. Predict the test set (majority class of the leaf, cut-off 0.5) and evaluate
test_pred <- predict(tree, test, type = "class")
conf_matrix <- table(Predicted = test_pred, Actual = test$Churn)
acc_test <- mean(test_pred == test$Churn)
acc_baseline <- mean(test$Churn == "No")
acc_train <- mean(predict(tree, train, type = "class") == train$Churn)
acc_full <- mean(predict(full, test, type = "class") == test$Churn)
conf_matrix; acc_test; acc_baseline; acc_train; acc_full

sensitivity <- conf_matrix["Yes", "Yes"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "Yes"]) # churners detected
specificity <- conf_matrix["No", "No"] / sum(conf_matrix[, "No"])   # stayers cleared
sensitivity; specificity

pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * x) # for easier writing in text section, shows percentages directly

# 8. Figure 1: the pruned tree
rpart.plot(tree, type = 2, extra = 106, under = TRUE, box.palette = "GnRd",
           fallen.leaves = TRUE, cex = 0.7)

# 9. Appendix A: cp table (Table A1) and variable importance (Table A2)
cp_rows <- cp_table[, "nsplit"] <= 25 | cp_table[, "nsplit"] == max(cp_table[, "nsplit"])
cp_summary <- data.frame(cp = sprintf("%.4f", cp_table[cp_rows, "CP"]),
                         Splits = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"],
                         Leaves = cp_table[cp_rows, "nsplit"] + 1,
                         round(cp_table[cp_rows, c("rel error", "xerror", "xstd")], 3))
names(cp_summary)[4:6] <- c("Training error", "CV error", "CV std. error")
knitr::kable(cp_summary, format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(Variable = names(var_importance),
                        `Importance (%)` = var_importance, check.names = FALSE),
             format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, row.names = FALSE)
\end{lstlisting}
